transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. Before we dive in, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Well, I'm here because... I just can't stop focusing on my jawline and my neck. There's this sagging, uneven area right there, and it's just all I can see. People tell me it looks fine, or normal, but I don't believe them. I feel like whenever I'm at work—I do personal care, so I'm around families and nurses a lot—or even just at church, it's the very first thing anyone notices about me. It just really bothers me.
On an average day, about how many hours would you say you spend thinking about your jawline and neck, or doing things like checking mirrors, camera angles, or trying to cover it up?

I'm not exactly sure on the total hours, but it's probably at least two or three hours a day if you add it all up. 

It really happens a lot before I go anywhere. Like, before I leave for work or a meeting, I just keep going back to the bathroom mirror. I'll stand there fixing my collar and trying to arrange my hair around my neck to see if I can hide it. Then I'll pull out my phone camera to take another look and check the angle. Sometimes I even ask my daughter if it looks strange... which I know frustrates her. Honestly, doing all that has made me late more than once.

When people reassure you that your jawline and neck look normal, is there any part of you that considers they might be right, or are you completely convinced that the flaw is really there exactly as you see it?

I don't really know for sure. I mean... I hear what they're saying. And maybe for a second I think, well, maybe it's not quite as bad as I think it is. But then I look in the mirror again, and it's just right there. It's so obvious to me. 

So... I guess I mostly just think they're being polite, or they just aren't looking at it as closely as I am. Because I can definitely see it, exactly how it is. It's really hard to just believe them when my own eyes are showing me something different.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a persistent, distressing preoccupation with a perceived defect in her jawline/neck that is not observable or only slight to others, accompanied by repetitive checking behaviors (mirror checking, camera angle checks, reassurance seeking) consuming over 2-3 hours daily, causing functional impairment (lateness, social distress). Insight is poor but not fully absent—she acknowledges intellectually that others may be right, but remains largely convinced her perceived flaw is real, consistent with BDD with poor insight rather than a delusional disorder (which would require complete conviction with no doubt) or generalized anxiety disorder (which lacks the specific appearance-focused preoccupation and repetitive behaviors).
